lessons.title: The Constitution of Cameroon in outline
lessons.programRef: GCE O Level Citizenship Education — The state, the Constitution, democracy (to be checked)
lessons.author: CastBridge (AI draft)
lessons.source: Original writing following the Cameroonian curriculum; to be reviewed by a teacher
objectives: Define a constitution and its role
Explain the separation of powers and name the main institutions
Describe the national symbols of Cameroon
Explain why the Constitution is the supreme law
reviewNotes: Teacher to verify with the current constitutional text: 1996 adoption, the description 'decentralised unitary state', names of the chambers and the Constitutional Council, flag description, motto wording, anthem title, National Day (20 May). Details on the powers of the President etc. are deliberately omitted.

Draft for teacher review: only widely accepted facts are used and the tone is neutral; the national symbols, institutions, legal ages and any health or legal statement must be verified before release. No political opinions are expressed.

blocks.md: A **constitution** is the highest law of a state. It sets out how the state is organised, the powers of its institutions, the rights and duties of citizens and how laws are made. All other laws must follow it. The Constitution of Cameroon was adopted in **1996** and has since been amended. It defines Cameroon as a **decentralised unitary state** with two official languages, English and French, with equal status.

blocks.caption: The three powers of the state
blocks.alt: A box 'Constitution' above three boxes: executive, legislative and judicial.

blocks.title: Separation of powers
blocks.md: Power is shared among three branches so that nobody has absolute power. The **executive** (the President and the Government) carries out the laws and runs public affairs. The **legislative** (Parliament: the **National Assembly** and the **Senate**) makes the laws and votes the budget. The **judiciary** (courts and judges) applies the law and settles disputes. In practice the branches cooperate and check each other.

Other institutions include the **Constitutional Council**, which checks that laws respect the Constitution, local councils and regional authorities in the decentralised state, and many public services. Public servants and officials must act according to the law. A citizen can seek justice from the courts.

blocks.title: National symbols
blocks.md:
- **The flag:** three vertical bands of green, red and yellow, with a yellow star in the middle of the red band.
- **The motto:** *Peace – Work – Fatherland*.
- **The anthem:** 'O Cameroon, Cradle of our Forefathers'.
- **The coat of arms.**
- **The capital:** Yaoundé. **National Day:** 20 May.
Symbols represent the unity and identity of the nation and must be respected.

blocks.title: Common mistakes
blocks.md:
- The Constitution is not an ordinary law; it is above all other laws.
- Separation of powers does not mean that the branches never work together.
- Learn the flag exactly: the star is on the red band, in the middle, and the bands are vertical. Write the motto with its three words in the right order.

blocks.title: Example 1: which branch?
blocks.statement: Which branch of government makes laws, which applies them in court, and which carries them out?
steps: Making laws is the work of the legislature.
Applying them in court is the work of the judiciary.
Carrying them out belongs to the executive.
blocks.answer: Legislature makes; judiciary applies in court; executive carries out.

blocks.title: Example 2: describe the flag
steps: The colours are green, red and yellow from left to right.
A yellow star is in the middle of the red band.
blocks.answer: Three vertical bands, green, red, yellow, with a yellow star on the red band.

lessons.title: Democracy and elections
lessons.programRef: GCE O Level Citizenship Education — The state, the Constitution, democracy (to be checked)
lessons.author: CastBridge (AI draft)
lessons.source: Original writing following the Cameroonian curriculum; to be reviewed by a teacher
objectives: Define democracy and describe its features
Explain the types and importance of elections
Describe how a free and fair election is organised
Explain the role of political parties and of the voter
reviewNotes: Teacher to verify: the types of elections and the names of institutions, the voting age and registration rules in the current electoral law, and neutral wording on opposition and parties. No electoral results or leaders are mentioned deliberately.

Draft for teacher review: only widely accepted facts are used and the tone is neutral; the national symbols, institutions, legal ages and any health or legal statement must be verified before release. No political opinions are expressed.

blocks.md: **Democracy** comes from Greek words meaning 'rule by the people'. In a democracy the people choose their leaders and take part in decisions. Features of democracy: free and fair **elections**, **rule of law**, **freedom of expression** and of the press, **respect for human rights**, equality before the law, the right to form political parties and associations, an independent justice system and the **peaceful transfer** of power.

blocks.caption: Steps of an election
blocks.alt: Four boxes with arrows: register, campaign and debate, vote in secret, count and announce results.

blocks.title: Types of elections
blocks.md:
- **Presidential** elections choose the head of state.
- **Legislative** elections choose members of the National Assembly.
- **Municipal** (local) elections choose councillors.
- Other elections choose senators through a different process. A **referendum** is a vote by the people on one question.

A **political party** is a group of people who share ideas on how to run the country and who try to win power through elections. Parties present programmes, campaign, and, if they win, govern; if they lose they form the opposition, which questions and checks the government. Citizens also form associations and unions.

blocks.title: A free and fair election
blocks.md:
1. Voters are **registered** on the electoral register and receive a voter's card.
2. Candidates and parties **campaign** according to the rules.
3. Voters choose by **secret ballot** at polling stations.
4. Votes are **counted** openly and results announced.
5. Complaints are heard by the competent court. An independent electoral body, with observers, helps to make the process credible.

blocks.title: Be careful
blocks.md:
- Voting is a right and a civic duty; it should be free: nobody may force, buy or threaten voters.
- A secret ballot protects the voter's choice.
- Democracy is not only voting day: it includes freedoms and the rule of law all year round.
- Rules about the voting age and registration are set by the electoral law; check them in your syllabus.

blocks.title: Example 1: steps
blocks.statement: Put in order: counting votes, registration of voters, voting, campaigning.
steps: Candidates campaign next, then people vote.

blocks.title: Example 2: why secret ballot?
blocks.statement: Explain why the ballot is secret.
steps: The voter's choice is a private decision.
Secrecy protects voters from pressure, threats or rewards.
So the result reflects free choice.
blocks.answer: To protect voters from pressure so that they choose freely.
